lesson.title: Divided by Distance: Allopatric Speciation
lesson.summary: Allopatric speciation is the formation of new species after a population is split by a geographic barrier that physically blocks gene flow, allowing the separated groups to diverge independently until reproductive isolation evolves.
lesson.body:
Allopatric speciation gets its name from Greek roots meaning "other" and "homeland," and the definition is straightforward: it is speciation that occurs when populations of the same species become geographically separated, so that gene flow between them is cut off or greatly reduced. Without gene flow linking their gene pools, the two populations are free to evolve independently, through natural selection adapting each one to its own local environment, through genetic drift causing random changes, and through the simple accumulation of different mutations over time. Given enough time and enough divergence, individuals from the two populations may eventually become unable to interbreed successfully even if they are later reunited, at which point speciation is complete.

The geographic barrier itself can take many forms. It might be a mountain range that rises between two areas, a new river channel, a change in sea level that splits a peninsula into islands, or in the classic textbook framing, a population that colonizes a remote island and becomes isolated from the mainland source population by open ocean. What all of these have in common is that they physically prevent individuals from meeting and mating, which is a different thing from the reproductive isolation you studied in the previous two chapters. Geographic separation on its own does not guarantee that the populations will become separate species, it only removes gene flow and gives evolutionary divergence the opportunity to proceed unopposed. Whether true reproductive isolation, prezygotic or postzygotic, actually evolves during that separation depends on how much time passes and how differently selection acts on each population.

One of the best documented real-world cases of allopatric speciation involves snapping shrimp in the genus Alpheus living on either side of the Isthmus of Panama. Before the isthmus fully closed, connecting North and South America and separating the Caribbean Sea from the Pacific Ocean, these shrimp formed continuous populations in what was then open water. Once the land bridge rose, roughly a few million years ago, though geologists continue to refine the exact timeline, it split the ancestral shrimp populations into a Caribbean side and a Pacific side. Researchers have identified multiple pairs of closely related Alpheus species, one member of each pair living in the Caribbean and the other in the Pacific, that are each other's closest relatives, more closely related to their counterpart across the isthmus than to any other shrimp in their own ocean. When scientists bring paired species together in the lab, most pairs show strong behavioral and, in more diverged pairs, physical barriers to successful mating, exactly the pattern you would expect if geographic isolation by the rising isthmus triggered independent evolution that eventually produced reproductive isolation.

A gentler, more classroom-familiar example is the finches Charles Darwin observed on the Galapagos Islands. A single ancestral finch population, blown or carried from the South American mainland, colonized the scattered islands of the archipelago. Because the islands are separated by open ocean, finches on different islands were largely cut off from interbreeding with each other, and each island population adapted somewhat differently to its own local food sources and conditions. Over generations this geographic isolation contributed to the buildup of differences among island populations, some of which eventually became distinct species. You will look much more closely at what happened to these finches ecologically in the chapter on adaptive radiation, but the geographic splitting itself, island by island, is a clear illustration of allopatric speciation in action.

It is worth being explicit about why allopatric speciation is considered the most common and most straightforward mode of speciation for biologists to document. Because it depends on a physical barrier to gene flow, it does not require explaining how reproductive isolation could evolve while two diverging populations are still in regular contact and capable of interbreeding, which as you will see in the next chapter is the much harder theoretical problem that sympatric speciation has to solve. This makes allopatric speciation, in some sense, the default expectation whenever biologists find two closely related species living in non-overlapping ranges separated by an obvious geographic barrier.
